CFBC · Pure Mathematics Unit 2 · Module 1, Chapter 4

Integration,
decoded

The biggest chapter in the module, and the one where the hard part is not the algebra but the choosing. This page is built around that: how to recognise what you are looking at, the four methods in the order you should try them, and fourteen tricks for forcing an integral that fits none of them into one that does.

The chapter

Every method, distilled

Seventeen cards in the same shape: the trigger, the rule, how to think about it, one worked example, and where it goes wrong. Six of them carry a concept check — answer it before moving on.

First look

Before you pick a method, look for the shape you already know.

The order to try things

When you see: Any integral, before you commit to a method

Integration is guess-and-check with very good guesses. Work down this list and stop at the first thing that fits — the methods get slower as you go, so never start at the bottom.

1. Recognition
2. Algebra
3. Substitution
4. By parts
How to think about it
  • Recognition is not a lesser method — it is the fastest one. can be done by partial fractions, but recognition takes one line.
  • Most marks are lost by reaching for by parts too early. If the derivative of one factor is sitting next to it, substitution is quicker and safer.
  • If nothing fits, do algebra first and ask again. Simplifying is not a detour; it is usually the method.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Starting with by parts on everything
It is the slowest method and often makes the integral worse. It is fourth on the list for a reason.
×  Not looking for first
A huge number of exam integrals are this pattern in disguise.
Concept check

Connects to: Everything below. This card is the map.

Standard forms

When you see: A single recognisable function

These are the integrals you must produce without thinking. Note the pattern running through them: a linear inside anything just divides the answer by .

  • Learn the two inverse-trig forms as a pair: a square root underneath gives , no root gives .

×  Losing the

Connects to: Every other method ends by landing on one of these.

The three golden patterns

When you see: A function and (a multiple of) its own derivative, together

These three cover an enormous share of exam integrals. Each one is the chain rule reversed — spot the inside function and its derivative sitting beside it, and the answer writes itself.

Log pattern
Power pattern
Exponential pattern
How to think about it
  • Ask one question: is the rest of the integrand the derivative of the awkward part? If yes — up to a constant — you are done in one line.
  • The constant never blocks you. If you need and only have , write and carry on.
  • These are exactly substitution with the working left out. When you are unsure, do the substitution; when you are confident, write the answer.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Using the log pattern when the top is not the derivative
works, but does not — that one needs division first.
×  Forgetting the minus sign
The derivative of is . That sign has to go somewhere.
Concept check

Connects to: The fast version of substitution. If you cannot see it, substitute.

Substitution

Change the variable so the integral becomes a standard form.

Choosing the substitution

When you see: A messy chunk — inside a root, a bracket, an exponent or a denominator

This is the real skill. Substitution works when the integrand contains some chunk and that chunk's derivative, up to a constant. Your job is to spot the chunk.

Where to look
The test
Typical choices
How to think about it
  • Always pick the innermost messy thing, then check whether its derivative is present. If it is not, that chunk is the wrong choice — try another.
  • A single stray multiplying everything is the classic signal for (something with ). A stray points at ; a stray points at .
  • If the derivative is not present at all, substitution will not help. Go to by parts, or to algebra.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Choosing to be the whole integrand
Then involves the product rule and you have made it worse.
×  Choosing a chunk whose derivative is nowhere to be seen
Substitution cannot invent the missing factor. Change your choice, or change your method.
Concept check

Connects to: The engine behind the three golden patterns.

Doing a substitution properly

When you see: You have chosen and are about to rewrite the integral

Three things must change, not one. Every in the integral has to disappear — the , the functions, and (for a definite integral) the limits.

Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
How to think about it
  • If a single survives into your -integral, something has gone wrong. Stop and find it.
  • Treat as a fraction here. becomes , which is exactly the swap you need.
  • For an indefinite integral, always convert back to at the end. An answer left in is incomplete.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Changing the function but not the
The is part of the integral. Forgetting it loses a factor and the answer is wrong.
×  Leaving the answer in terms of
Unless you changed the limits, you must convert back.

Connects to: Leftover handles the case where Step 2 does not finish cleanly.

Definite integrals: change the limits

When you see: A substitution inside

The limits are values of . Once you switch to , they must become values of — or you have to convert the whole answer back before substituting them.

Convert them
Then never look back
If the limits reverse
How to think about it
  • Changing the limits is almost always faster than converting back — and there is one less place to make a mistake.
  • Write beside each limit as you convert. Label them, or you will substitute the -limits into a -integral.
  • A decreasing substitution (like ) flips the order of the limits. Swap them and change the sign.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Keeping the -limits with a -integrand
Guaranteed wrong answer, and an easy one for a marker to spot.
×  Converting back and re-substituting anyway
Legal, just slower. Pick one route and be consistent.

Connects to: Applies to every substitution in Part 2.

By parts

For products that substitution cannot touch.

By parts: the formula and the choice

When you see: A product of two functions that are unrelated to each other

By parts comes straight from the product rule. It trades your integral for a different one — so the entire skill is choosing and so that the new integral is easier.

The formula
Choose by LIATE
The rule of thumb
How to think about it
  • LIATE: whichever type appears first in that list becomes . In , Algebraic beats Exponential, so .
  • Test your choice before committing: if looks worse than what you started with, you chose the wrong way round.
  • In the wrong choice gives — the power went up. That is the signal to swap.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Choosing to be the part that gets worse
If differentiating makes it more complicated, you have them the wrong way round.
×  Using by parts when substitution would work
is not a by-parts question — the is the derivative of the exponent, so it is recognition.
Concept check

Connects to: Compare with substitution — the two-ways section shows integrals where either works.

The trick

When you see: A single function you cannot integrate: , ,

There is no product to split — so invent one. Write the function as itself times , and let the be the part you integrate.

The move
Which gives
Result
How to think about it
  • This is the only way to integrate , , and . They are on the syllabus precisely because of this trick.
  • LIATE agrees with it: L and I are first in the list, so they always become — even when there is nothing else in sight.
  • The integral you are left with is usually a golden pattern. For you get , which is after fixing the constant.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Trying to integrate directly
There is no standard form for it. The trick is the method.
×  Letting the be
Then and you learn nothing. The is always the part you integrate.

Connects to: A special case of by parts, and the reason LIATE starts with L and I.

By parts twice — and the loop

When you see: , , or

Two different situations look the same. With a power out front, repeating by parts grinds the power down to nothing. With two functions that never simplify, the integral comes back — and that is a feature, not a failure.

Grinding down
The loop
Solve for
How to think about it
  • A power of tells you how many times you will apply the rule: means twice, means three times.
  • In the loop case you must keep the same choice of both times. Swapping halfway sends you back to where you started — the famous .
  • When the original integral reappears, give it a name at the very beginning. Writing first makes the final step obvious.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Swapping and on the second pass
You undo the first application exactly and arrive at .
×  Forgetting the after dividing by
It is still an indefinite integral.

Connects to: The hardest by-parts questions in the chapter, and both are formulaic.

Rational functions

Fractions: split them, or complete the square.

Partial fractions inside an integral

When you see: A rational function with a factorisable denominator

Chapter 3 was the preparation; this is the payoff. Split the fraction, and every piece becomes a logarithm, a power, or an arctangent.

Split, then integrate
Each piece
Improper first
How to think about it
  • Run the same two gates as in Chapter 3: proper first, factorised second. An improper fraction must be divided or nothing works.
  • A repeated factor does not give a log. integrates to a negative power, and mixing that up is a common slip.
  • A quadratic factor gives , which splits again: the part is and gives a log, the part gives an arctangent.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Integrating before splitting
There is no standard form for the unsplit fraction.
×  Expecting every piece to be a log
Only the pieces are. Squared factors and quadratic factors behave differently.

Connects to: Chapter 3, put to work. The whole reason you learnt it.

Completing the square

When you see: A quadratic denominator that will not factorise

When partial fractions is unavailable, force the quadratic into the shape of a standard inverse-trig form. Completing the square is what does the forcing.

Target shapes
The move
With a minus in front
How to think about it
  • Decide first which shape you are heading for: a square root underneath means , no root means .
  • is a substitution, but it is so simple you can do it in your head — , so nothing else changes.
  • Check the discriminant before completing the square. If the quadratic does factorise, partial fractions is faster.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Completing the square on a quadratic that factorises
Check first. If it is positive, use partial fractions.
×  Losing the in the arctangent form
here, so the answer carries a .
Concept check

Connects to: Pairs with partial fractions: factorisable goes one way, irreducible the other.

Trigonometry

Identities first, integration second.

Even powers of sine and cosine

When you see: , ,

You cannot integrate directly. The double-angle identities turn a squared trig function into something linear in , which you can integrate on sight.

The two identities
Result
Fourth powers
How to think about it
  • Remember which identity carries the minus: takes . Mixing them up is the single most common error here.
  • The identity is the method. Once it is applied there is nothing left but standard forms.
  • For you apply the identity twice: once to square it, then again on the that appears.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Writing
The power rule applies to , not to . There is no present to make it a golden pattern.
×  Getting the sign of the identity wrong
takes the minus. Check it at : and . ✓

Connects to: Contrast with odd powers, which need a completely different move.

Odd powers of sine and cosine

When you see: , ,

An odd power hands you a spare factor. Split one off, convert what remains using , and the spare factor becomes exactly the derivative you need.

Split off one
Then it is a golden pattern
Same for cosine
How to think about it
  • Odd power → split one off. Even power → double angle. That one sentence decides every question in this section.
  • The spare factor always pairs with the other function: split off a , substitute . That is what makes the derivative appear.
  • — same move, then expand.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Splitting off from an even power
leaves , which is not the derivative of anything useful. Even powers need the double angle.
×  Forgetting to expand
is easiest term by term.
Concept check

Connects to: The mirror image of even powers.

Products of sines and cosines

When you see: , — different angles multiplied

A product of trig functions at different angles cannot be integrated as it stands. The product-to-sum formulae turn the product into a sum, and a sum is trivial.

The four formulae
How to think about it
  • Look at the angles. Same angle multiplied () is a golden pattern; different angles () needs product-to-sum.
  • Every formula has a factor of on the left, so your answer always picks up a . Do not lose it.
  • Only the two signs differ between the four formulae. Learn the sine pair and the cosine pair, and check a sign by testing .
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Integrating the product term by term
. There is no product rule for integration.
×  Dropping the
The identities are stated for , so halve at the end.

Connects to: The last of the identity-first techniques.

How to study this

Learning it, and keeping it

Eight habits for the biggest chapter in the module. None of them involve rereading the notes.

Work down the list, never up

Recognition, then algebra, then substitution, then by parts. Most wasted time in this chapter comes from starting at the bottom — reaching for by parts on an integral that recognition would have finished in one line.

Try this: Before writing anything, say out loud which of the four you are using and why. If you cannot say why, you have not looked hard enough for a faster route.

Ask one question about every fraction

Is the top the derivative of the bottom? If yes, it is a logarithm and you are done. That single question resolves a surprising share of exam integrals, including ones that look like partial fractions questions.

Try this: Take any twenty integrals from the exercises and answer only that question for each. Two minutes, and it rewires how you look at fractions.

A missing constant is never a reason to stop

You need and have ? Multiply inside by and divide outside by . You need and have ? Same move. Constants are free — only the shape matters.

Try this: Practise writing as a reflex, without thinking about it.

Differentiate your answer back

Integration is the one topic where you can check yourself completely. Differentiating your answer must return the integrand — not something like it, exactly it.

Try this: Do this on every question you practise until it becomes automatic. It catches missing constants, lost minus signs and forgotten chain-rule factors.

Learn LIATE and trust it

Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential. Whichever comes first is . The wrong choice often cannot be finished at all, not merely slowly — so this is not a preference, it is the method.

Try this: Test it: try the wrong way round and see how quickly you get stuck.

For trigonometry, read the power before anything else

Even power means double angle. Odd power means split one off. Powers of tan mean . Different angles multiplied mean product-to-sum. Four rules, and they never overlap.

Try this: Write those four lines on one card. That card is the entire trig section of this chapter.

When stuck, do algebra

Divide it, split it, complete the square, apply an identity, multiply by a clever . Every one of these turns an impossible integral into a standard form. The algebra is not a detour — for many questions it is the method.

Try this: Go through the forcing toolkit above and, for each trick, find one integral in the exercises where it is the key move.

Keep an error log

In this chapter the mistakes are highly repetitive: a lost , a missing , -limits left on a -integral, a sign dropped from . Write down which one caught you each time.

Try this: After a week you will find you make two or three errors, over and over. Those are worth more attention than any new technique.
